query: For additively manufactured high-entropy-alloy components, what single intervention could improve dimensional precision and mechanical integrity while reducing fabrication-induced defects? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the current fabrication baseline, defines the processing and application conditions under which it should hold, identifies supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) of face-centered-cubic (FCC) high-entropy alloys, replacing the standard Gaussian laser spot with a spatially homogenized (top-hat) beam profile will simultaneously improve dimensional precision and mechanical integrity by stabilizing conduction-mode melting and suppressing spatter and pore formation, thereby reducing porosity and residual-stress-driven distortion relative to a Gaussian-beam baseline at matched volumetric energy density.
generation.material_initial_state: Gas-atomized, pre-alloyed FCC HEA powder (e.g., CoCrFeMnNi-like chemistry), 15–45 µm particle size distribution, low oxygen content (<200 ppm), standard LPBF platform using a Gaussian beam as the current baseline; virgin powder for the initial build.
generation.intervention: Implement a top-hat (spatially homogenized) laser beam profile for all scan vectors during LPBF, holding the nominal volumetric energy density constant relative to the Gaussian-beam baseline.
generation.conditions: LPBF in argon with O2 <100 ppm; layer thickness 30–50 µm; laser power 200–350 W; scan speed 0.8–1.2 m/s; hatch spacing 80–120 µm; build plate preheat 150–200 °C; FCC HEA compositions with demonstrated weldability (e.g., CoCrFeMnNi-type); part heights ≤20 mm; geometries include thin-walled (≤1 mm) and bulk coupons; standard stripe or chessboard scan strategies without interlayer remelting or other auxiliary treatments.
generation.structural_mediator: A more uniform, shallow conduction-mode melt pool with reduced peak irradiance, lower recoil pressure, and suppressed spatter/denudation, yielding smoother interlayer topography and reduced populations of lack-of-fusion and keyhole pores; accompanying reduction in residual stress gradients and distortion upon baseplate release.
generation.mechanism: The top-hat beam lowers the peak intensity and homogenizes lateral energy input, avoiding localized boiling and keyhole instability that drive pore formation and spatter. Uniform track width and depth improve hatch overlap and interlayer planarity, reducing geometric overbuild/undercut and initiation sites for lack-of-fusion defects. Lower defect density and more uniform thermal history decrease residual stresses and stabilize geometry. The resulting higher density and smoother surfaces translate into improved tensile ductility and fatigue performance without sacrificing strength.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to a Gaussian-beam LPBF baseline at matched volumetric energy density, parts built with a top-hat beam will exhibit: (1) lower volumetric porosity; (2) reduced dimensional deviation from CAD for both thin-walled and bulk features; (3) lower as-built top-surface roughness; (4) equal or higher yield/ultimate strength with higher elongation-to-failure and improved fatigue life; and (5) reduced distortion after baseplate release. The direction of change is expected to be beneficial on all listed metrics and practically measurable; the exact magnitude depends on alloy and process window and is not specified here.
generation.baseline: Conventional LPBF of the same FCC HEA using a Gaussian laser beam profile and process parameters tuned for near-full density, without beam shaping or interlayer remelting.
generation.boundary: Benefits may be minimal if the Gaussian-beam process is already operating in a highly stable conduction mode with negligible spatter and porosity. For alloys with strong intrinsic hot-cracking susceptibility or for refractory HEAs requiring very high energy input, beam shaping alone may not suppress defects. At extreme volumetric energy densities that inherently cause keyholing or lack-of-fusion regardless of spot profile, or in environments with elevated oxygen or poor powder quality that dominate defect formation, the hypothesis may not hold.
generation.uncertainty: Quantitative effect sizes for HEA-specific systems under the stated conditions are uncertain without alloy- and geometry-specific datasets. The influence of beam shaping on grain size and texture in different HEAs may vary, which could modulate mechanical outcomes.

falsification_experiment.design: Print matched sets of HEA coupons and thin-walled features on the same LPBF machine under identical conditions, varying only the beam profile: Gaussian (baseline) vs top-hat (intervention), with matched volumetric energy density and scan strategy. Use fresh powder from the same lot and replicate n ≥ 5 specimens per condition. After stress-relief-free builds, assess porosity, dimensional accuracy, surface roughness, residual stress/distortion, microstructure, tensile properties, and high-cycle fatigue.
measurements: Volumetric porosity via high-resolution X-ray CT on bulk and thin-walled regions
Dimensional deviation from CAD via 3D structured-light or CT metrology on thin walls and boss/slot features
As-built top-surface roughness Sa/Sz via optical profilometry
Residual stress (XRD sin²ψ) and post-release distortion measured optically
Melt pool cross-sections for pore morphology and track overlap; EBSD for grain size/texture
Room-temperature tensile properties (YS, UTS, uniform and total elongation) on standard mini-tensile coupons
High-cycle fatigue life (R = 0.1 or −1) on polished specimens to isolate internal-defect effects
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: At matched volumetric energy density and within the stated conditions, the hypothesis is falsified if the top-hat beam does not simultaneously produce statistically significant reductions (p < 0.05, two-sample tests) in both (a) CT-measured volumetric porosity and (b) dimensional deviation from CAD, relative to the Gaussian baseline. It is also falsified if tensile ductility or fatigue life are significantly worse with the top-hat beam while porosity and dimensional deviation show no significant improvement.
